title: C6H6 next-hour prediction - Italy (UCI Air Quality)
summary: We predicted C6H6 one hour ahead using the Italy (UCI Air Quality) data. Random Forest did best on the validation period, so we used it. On the test period (16 Jan 2005 to 4 Apr 2005) its average error was 1.710 µg/m³. Just repeating the last hour's value gave 2.291 µg/m³, so the model was 25.4% better. 33 episodes were flagged: 19 look like unusual pollution, 1 look like data problems and 13 are unclear. Its prediction was within 20% of the real value in 55% of the test hours. Mild overfitting: the error on new data is somewhat higher than on the data it learned from, once you allow for the test period being 18% easier to predict. Some gap is normal, and the settings were picked on separate data, so the test score is still a fair one.
how_it_was_made: Read the hourly data and treated empty cells and -200 as missing.

Built the inputs: hour, weekday, the reading 1 hour before, the reading 2 hours before, the reading 3 hours before, the reading at the same time the day before, temperature, relative humidity, absolute humidity.
Split the timeline in order: first 60% to train, next 20% to choose the model, last 20% to test.
Tried Linear Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, each with a few settings that keep it from memorising the training hours. Each predicts how much the level changes in the next hour.
Checked for overfitting: compared the chosen model's average error on the hours it learned from with its error on the test hours, allowing for some periods being harder to predict than others.

Counted the test hours where the prediction was within 20% of the real value. Readings below the 10th percentile were measured against that percentile, so tiny misses on near-zero readings don't count as big ones.
Flagged test hours where the miss was more than 7.36 µg/m³ (bigger than 95% of the misses on the validation period).
By design this limit flags 5% of the validation hours; on the test period it flagged 2.2% of hours. So the number of episodes partly depends on where the limit is set.

Grouped flagged hours that were less than 3 hours apart and checked each group: missing inputs or a gap, a stuck reading, or a sudden jump that nothing else shared mean a data problem; other pollutants moving the same way at the same time mean unusual pollution; anything else is unclear.
patterns: Most episodes peaked around 09:00, 18:00 and 20:00, and 85% fell on weekdays, more than the 71% you'd expect, so they lean towards working days. The busiest month was Mar 2005 with 17 episodes.
